strengths: Addresses a relevant problem: improving online RL sample efficiency using reward-free, mixed-quality offline trajectories from multiple embodiments.

Reports substantial empirical gains across 72 pixel-based control tasks. At 150k interactions, GSA achieves approximately 75% Meta-World success and 631 average DMControl return, substantially exceeding the reported training-from-scratch baselines.

The combination of world-model pre-training, retrieved experience replay, and behavioral-cloning guidance is practical and clearly motivated. Component ablations provide evidence that guidance helps on difficult manipulation tasks.
Provides per-task results, computational costs, pseudocode, and many architectural and optimization details.
weaknesses: The contribution is primarily a combination of established techniques: RSSM pre-training, experience replay, nearest-neighbor retrieval, and JSRL-like behavioral guidance. The experiments do not sufficiently isolate the value of the proposed combination: missing controls include pre-training plus guidance without rehearsal, guidance without pre-training, and retrieved versus random or task-filtered replay.

The strongest comparison spans 72 tasks only against methods trained from scratch. Competing methods using offline data are evaluated on a small selected subset. The iVideoGPT comparison imports results from another paper with different pre-training data and training procedures, so it cannot isolate the benefit of GSA's adaptation method. Model-size and computational matching are also insufficiently established.

The theoretical analysis is unsound as written. Proposition 1 assumes proximity of retrieved states, whereas the algorithm retrieves entire trajectories using initial-image similarity; its expected Euclidean distance is also incorrectly called total variation. Proposition 2 offers a regularization intuition rather than a forgetting guarantee. Proposition 3 incorrectly derives a mixture-policy identity from a coupling condition and does not analyze the actual temporally extended switching policy.

The claimed diagnosis of distribution shift as the root cause is not established by a t-SNE visualization and distance measurements on one task. Direct measurements of prediction degradation, forgetting, and their relationship to policy performance are missing. Execution guidance does not explicitly estimate world-model confidence despite being described as steering toward high-confidence regions.

The breadth of the 'non-curated' setting is overstated. Meta-World data are deliberately generated from task-trained policies on all 50 evaluation tasks with injected noise. One world model is trained per benchmark, and no controlled comparison establishes the benefit of sharing across embodiments. These experiments support reuse of in-domain data more strongly than generalist transfer.

Result reporting contains material inconsistencies. Averaging the available task entries in Tables 2–3 gives approximately 0.656 for Dreamer v3 at 1M steps, rather than the reported 0.900, and approximately 0.430 for DrQ v2 at 150k, rather than 0.442. Door Close lacks baseline results. The headline 102.8% aggregate improvement needs an explicit aggregation definition and reconciled tables.

Reproducibility remains incomplete: retrieval count, behavioral-cloning training budget, and guidance start-time/duration distributions are not specified adequately. Algorithm 1's guidance interval conflicts with the stated duration interpretation. Three seeds and missing uncertainty estimates in the full result tables further limit confidence in task-level comparisons.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful problem: improving online RL sample efficiency using reward-free, mixed-quality data from multiple embodiments. Reusing this data during adaptation is practically motivated.

The evaluation is broad: 72 pixel-based control tasks across six embodiments, with three seeds per task. Reported improvements over training from scratch are substantial, particularly on difficult manipulation and quadruped tasks.

GSA combines established components into a coherent pipeline: world-model pre-training, retrieval-based rehearsal, and behavioral-cloning guidance. The component ablations provide evidence that rehearsal and guidance improve performance beyond pre-training alone on the tested tasks.
The appendices provide task-level results, implementation details, hyperparameters, and compute estimates, and explicitly acknowledge limitations concerning in-domain data and unseen embodiments.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is limited and insufficiently isolated. The main components closely resemble established experience replay, nearest-neighbor retrieval, and JSRL-style policy guidance. The ablations omit pre-training plus guidance without rehearsal, random versus retrieved rehearsal, and matched single-embodiment pre-training. Consequently, they do not establish which distinctive aspects of GSA are necessary or whether multi-embodiment pre-training contributes beyond access to relevant offline trajectories.

The strongest comparisons are not sufficiently controlled. The 72-task evaluation primarily compares against agents without offline data; offline-data baselines and component ablations cover much smaller subsets. Section 4.1 imports iVideoGPT results from another paper despite differences in pre-training data and training procedures, preventing clean attribution of the gains. Appendix G also substantially modifies ExPLORe after unsuccessful tuning. Matched data, model capacity, and training settings are needed to substantiate superiority over competing adaptation approaches.

The theoretical analysis contains substantive errors. Proposition 1 assumes distance-based selection of individual states, whereas the algorithm retrieves whole trajectories using their initial observations; its conclusion therefore does not follow for the implemented retrieval procedure. It also incorrectly calls expected Euclidean distance total variation. Proposition 2 offers an intuition about regularization rather than a guarantee against forgetting. Proposition 3 incorrectly derives a fixed policy mixture from an alpha-coupling condition, and its proof does not cover the implemented temporally extended switching schedule. Its uniformly positive guide-advantage assumption is also unverified for mixed-quality data.

The claimed causal diagnosis of distribution shift and catastrophic forgetting is stronger than the evidence. Figure 2 shows a distribution visualization and distance comparison for Shelf Place, but does not directly measure prediction degradation, retention of offline dynamics, or model confidence. Improved returns after adding rehearsal and guidance cannot alone distinguish reduced forgetting from better exploration or more informative rollout starting states.

The generality of the non-curated-data claim is limited. Meta-World data is deliberately collected from trained policies for all 50 evaluated tasks, with Gaussian action noise added. This is a useful reward-free adaptation setting, but it does not demonstrate robustness to arbitrary mixtures, irrelevant trajectories, or absent target-task coverage. There are no systematic quality-mixture or held-out-embodiment experiments.

The reported aggregates need correction and clarification. Recomputing the Dreamer v3 at 1M mean from the 49 available Meta-World task entries gives approximately 0.656, not the 0.900 reported in Table 3. The corresponding DrQ v2 at 150k entries average approximately 0.430, rather than 0.442. Door Close lacks baseline results, and the handling of this missing task and the calculation underlying the headline 102.8% improvement are insufficiently specified. These discrepancies reduce confidence in the quantitative summary, although the task-level results still indicate substantial gains.

Several details necessary for reproduction remain unclear, including the number of retrieved trajectories, behavior-cloning training budget, and distributions governing guidance start times and durations. Algorithm 1 also tests k <= t <= H despite describing H as a duration. Baseline parameter counts and comparable compute costs are not established. These gaps, together with the comparison and theoretical issues, leave the submission below the acceptance threshold despite its promising empirical results.

strengths: Addresses a practically relevant problem: improving online RL using reward-free, mixed-quality, multi-embodiment offline trajectories.

Reports substantial sample-efficiency gains across 72 simulated visuomotor tasks. At 150k interactions, GSA achieves approximately 75% Meta-World success and 631 average DMControl return, substantially exceeding the reported training-from-scratch baselines.

The integration of world-model pre-training, retrieved experience rehearsal, and behavior-cloned execution guidance is understandable and practical. Component ablations provide evidence that rehearsal and guidance improve upon pre-training alone.
The appendix includes per-task results, architecture details, hyperparameters, pseudocode, and compute estimates.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is limited relative to existing replay-based offline-to-online RL and jump-start exploration. The experiments do not sufficiently isolate the distinctive contributions: there are no controlled comparisons of retrieved versus random or task-filtered replay, generalist versus task-specific pre-training, or mid-episode guidance versus otherwise identical JSRL-style guidance. Rehearsal also bundles model training and imagination-state augmentation without separating their effects.

The strongest comparative claims lack controlled evaluation. The 72-task evaluation primarily compares against training from scratch; offline-data competitors are evaluated on a much smaller subset. The iVideoGPT curves are imported from another paper with different data and training protocols. Model capacity and compute are not clearly matched to the 280M-parameter GSA model, limiting attribution of improvements.

The proposed explanation of distribution shift as the root cause is stronger than the evidence. Figure 2 provides a single-task visualization and distance comparison, but there are no direct measurements of prediction degradation, forgetting, or confidence calibration. Behavior cloning does not explicitly select states by world-model confidence, despite that characterization of execution guidance.

Appendix B contains substantive theoretical gaps. Proposition 1 calls expected Euclidean distance 'total variation' and assumes state-level proximity that retrieval using only initial trajectory observations does not guarantee. Proposition 2 supplies an intuition rather than a forgetting bound. Proposition 3 incorrectly uses an alpha-coupling condition to infer a fixed policy mixture; this also does not model the implemented temporally extended switching policy.

The scope of 'non-curated' data needs stronger qualification. Meta-World data are deliberately generated from trained task policies across the same 50 evaluation tasks, with injected action noise. This is a useful reward-unlabeled setting, but robustness to naturally heterogeneous data, poor-quality-only data, or held-out manipulation tasks remains unestablished.

Reproducibility and reporting require correction. Retrieval count, behavior-cloning training budget, and guidance interval sampling are unspecified. Pre-training is described as 150k steps in Appendix F but 200k in Table 5. Table 3 reports a DreamerV3 1M-step mean of 0.900, whereas averaging the 49 available task entries gives approximately 0.656. Missing baseline entries and only three seeds further warrant clearer aggregation and uncertainty reporting.

strengths: Addresses a useful problem: improving online RL with reward-free, mixed-quality, multi-embodiment offline trajectories. The pipeline is straightforward and practically motivated.

Substantial empirical gains across 72 simulated pixel-control tasks. At 150k online steps, NCRL achieves 74.8% mean success on Meta-World versus 43.0% for DrQ-v2 and 36.0% for DreamerV3; its mean DMControl return is 617.7 versus 226.5 and 320.9, respectively.

The evaluation includes several offline-data baselines, an aligned iVideoGPT comparison, component ablations, retrieval-quality experiments, and guidance-schedule sensitivity tests. These provide meaningful evidence that the combined method improves sample efficiency.
The appendix supplies per-task results, learning curves, pseudocode, architecture details, hyperparameters, and compute estimates.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is limited: NCRL combines an existing RSSM with nearest-neighbor retrieval, offline replay, and behavior-cloned policy guidance closely related to JSRL. The experiments do not isolate the benefit of random mid-episode switching over JSRL-style switching within the same model-based backbone, or separate rehearsal's model-retention and rollout-initialization effects.

The broadest comparison is against training-from-scratch methods with smaller models, whereas offline-data competitors are evaluated on selected task subsets. Appendix A.5 controls DreamerV3 model size on only two locomotion tasks. Thus, the 72-task aggregate does not establish similarly broad superiority over equally sized, pretrained competitors.

The claimed causal explanation is insufficiently established. Figure 2's single-task distribution visualization and distance measurements do not demonstrate that distribution shift or catastrophic forgetting causes fine-tuning failure. Direct measurements of dynamics prediction error, retained offline performance, and their relationship to downstream returns are missing. Execution guidance also does not explicitly estimate world-model confidence.

The theoretical analysis overstates its conclusions. Proposition 1 assumes closeness of retrieved states, while the implemented method retrieves entire trajectories using initial-image similarity; the assumption need not hold along those trajectories. Expected Euclidean distance is also incorrectly called total variation. Proposition 2 analyzes a stationary action mixture rather than the implemented temporally contiguous switching scheme, and its lower bound need not be positive. The subsequent sufficient condition for positive improvement has the wrong sign.

The non-curated-data claim has restricted scope. Meta-World data are deliberately generated using task-trained TDMPC-v2 policies with injected noise across the evaluation tasks. Poor imitation performance does not establish independence from successful trajectories. Held-out-task and successful-trajectory-removal experiments would better establish the claimed breadth of applicability; multi-embodiment training alone does not demonstrate cross-embodiment transfer.

Reproducibility has unresolved inconsistencies: the main text reports three seeds, whereas Appendix I reports five NCRL seeds; compute estimates use 150k pretraining updates while Table 6 specifies 200k. The retrieval count and guidance start/duration sampling distributions are not clearly specified. Together with the incomplete controls and unsupported mechanistic claims, these issues leave an otherwise promising empirical contribution slightly below the acceptance threshold.

strengths: Addresses a useful practical problem: improving online RL sample efficiency using reward-free, mixed-quality offline trajectories.
Reports substantial gains across 72 simulated tasks. At 150k online samples, NCRL achieves 74.8% mean Meta-World success versus 43.0% for DrQ-v2 and 36.0% for DreamerV3.

The experimental effort includes component ablations, retrieval precision, sensitivity to irrelevant data, an aligned iVideoGPT comparison, and limited model-size controls. These provide meaningful evidence that the complete pipeline is effective.
The appendix provides pseudocode, architecture details, hyperparameters, computational requirements, and per-task results.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is limited: NCRL combines a scaled Dreamer-style world model, nearest-neighbor retrieval, offline replay, and behavior-cloned execution guidance closely related to JSRL. The experiments do not sufficiently isolate the contribution beyond this combination, particularly against the same world-model backbone with JSRL-style guidance or guidance without rehearsal.

The central causal explanation is insufficiently established. Figure 2 shows distribution differences on one task, but does not directly measure prediction degradation or catastrophic forgetting. Experience rehearsal simultaneously changes model training, imagination starting states, and guidance data, leaving their effects entangled. Figure 6 shows guidance driving the manipulation gains, which also supports a simpler exploration explanation.

The theoretical analysis does not establish the stated guarantees for the implemented algorithm. Proposition 1 assumes threshold-based selection of individual states, whereas the method retrieves entire trajectories using initial-image similarity; its expected pairwise distance is also incorrectly called total variation. Proposition 2 analyzes a stationary action mixture rather than contiguous, randomly timed guidance segments. The subsequent positivity condition has an incorrect sign, and nonnegative expected advantage alone does not guarantee strict improvement.

The broadest evaluation compares against training-from-scratch baselines with smaller models. Appendix A.5 addresses model size on only two locomotion tasks, while offline-data competitors are evaluated on small task subsets. These additional controls are useful but do not establish the headline advantage under consistently matched capacity and training protocols across the full benchmark.

The evidence supports a narrower data setting than the framing suggests. Meta-World data are deliberately generated from task-trained TDMPC-v2 policies with injected noise across the downstream tasks. Poor imitation-learning performance does not establish independence from successful trajectories. There is no systematic held-out-task or held-out-embodiment evaluation, and separate world models are trained per benchmark.

Several reporting issues weaken reproducibility and interpretation: the main text specifies three seeds while Appendix I specifies five for NCRL; pretraining is described as 150k steps in the compute section but 200k in the hyperparameter table; retrieval count and guidance-window sampling are not fully specified. Additionally, Figure 14 shows failure with 100% irrelevant data despite the accompanying broad robustness claim.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful problem: improving online RL with reward-free, mixed-quality offline trajectories. Combining world-model pretraining, retrieved experience rehearsal, and behavioral guidance yields a practical, coherent approach.

The empirical gains are substantial. Across 50 Meta-World tasks, NCRL achieves 74.8% mean success at 150k online steps versus 36.0% for DreamerV3 and 43.0% for DrQ-v2. Across 22 DMControl tasks, its mean return is approximately 618 versus 321 and 226, respectively.

The evaluation extends beyond scratch baselines to several methods using offline data. The appendix adds an aligned iVideoGPT comparison, model-size controls on two tasks, retrieval-quality experiments, and guidance-schedule sensitivity studies.

Component ablations support the usefulness of rehearsal and guidance, especially on difficult manipulation tasks. Detailed per-task results, pseudocode, hyperparameters, and compute estimates improve transparency.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is primarily an integration of established ingredients: Dreamer-style pretraining, nearest-neighbor retrieval, offline replay, and JSRL-like behavioral guidance. Important controls are missing, particularly an otherwise identical Dreamer agent with guidance but without pretraining, and separate ablations of rehearsal for model fitting versus imagined-rollout initialization. Consequently, the necessity of the proposed combination is not fully established.

The broadest comparisons are against scratch agents without offline data, while competing offline-data methods are evaluated on selected tasks. The 280M-parameter model is size-matched against DreamerV3 on only two locomotion tasks, leaving the full benchmark comparison partially confounded by capacity. The appendix strengthens the evaluation but does not resolve these issues across the headline results.

The non-curated-data claim needs qualification. Meta-World data are deliberately generated from task-trained TD-MPC2 agents across the same 50 evaluation tasks, with injected noise. This is useful reward-unlabeled data, but it retains substantial task-specific supervision through collection. There is no held-out manipulation-task or embodiment evaluation, and separate world models are trained per benchmark.

The distribution-shift explanation is plausible but not causally demonstrated. Figure 2 provides an illustrative visualization and distance comparison, without direct measurements establishing degraded predictive accuracy or catastrophic forgetting. Improved exploration and access to useful offline behaviors remain alternative explanations for the gains.

Appendix B overstates its theoretical support. Proposition 1 assumes threshold-based selection of nearby states, whereas the implementation retrieves complete trajectories using their initial observations; the assumed ordering need not hold for subsequent states. Expected Euclidean distance is also incorrectly called total variation. Proposition 2 concerns a stationary action mixture rather than the implemented contiguous guidance interval, and its subsequent positivity condition has a sign error. A better guide policy does not by itself establish the claimed improvement.

Several reporting details need correction: Section 4 specifies three seeds, whereas Appendix I reports five for NCRL; the retrieval count and guidance-interval sampling distributions are not clearly specified; and Figure 14's complete failure with 100% irrelevant data contradicts its unqualified robustness description. These ambiguities reduce reproducibility and confidence in the broader claims.
